Why can density flatten without dissipation?

On the periodic interval x∈[0,1], let Gσ(v)=exp(−v²/(2σ²))/(√(2π)σ). The exact force-free solution is f=Gσ(v)[1+a cos(2π(x−vt))]. Each velocity carries its own position pattern. It satisfies ∂tf+v∂xf=0.

Integrating over ALL velocities givesρ=1+D cos(2πx), D=a exp(−2π²σ²t²). Faster velocity spread mixes the position mode sooner. Total mass stays1, and ∫∫f² dx dv=(1+a²/2)/(2√πσ) stays constant in time. This quadratic norm is NOT kinetic energy. A flatter density does not mean the full distribution has become uniform.

The left ink reads q=√(2π)σf on a fixed0–2 ruler, rather than scaling to its current peak. Unbounded Gaussian tails are omitted only from the drawing. Finite cell-centre samples can miss between-cell structure. Small positive D uses scientific notation even when the density readout rounds to1. x1 is the same periodic position as x0.

This independently authored bounded example has no self-consistent fields, collisions or relativity. It is not Vlasov–Maxwell regularity, nonlinear Landau damping, plasma stability, spin-glass/Boltzmann/NLS research, a manuscript or Lean fidelity audit. It validates none of the episode’s research claims.
